evidence_spans: There were 4 different regions identified in the cross-sectional microstructure, i.e. oxide layer (OL), internal oxidation depth (IOD), internal nitridation depth (IND) and substrate.
According to EDS mapping, neither continuous Al 2 O 3 nor Cr 2 O 3 layer was found on the alloy surface after 200 hours of oxidation at 1000 °C.
Instead, Al segregated near the top surface, while Cr distribution was almost uniform in the OL.

evidence_spans: The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration.

Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure.
Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h.

cross_paper_synthesis.consensus: Both papers address the reliability of oxidation kinetics data by explicitly stating how mass gain values were derived (normalization) and how uncertainty was represented (error bars from repeated measurements).
cross_paper_synthesis.different_approaches: One paper focuses on the definition of error bars as a statistical metric of repeatability, while the other focuses on the units of the reported data (area normalization) and explicitly notes the absence of specific geometric details in the provided text.
cross_paper_synthesis.condition_dependencies: The quantification of deviation via error bars is linked to repeated measurements under specific oxidation conditions (1000 °C, air, 200 hours) in one case, whereas the area normalization is a general reporting standard for the specific dataset in the other case.
cross_paper_synthesis.contradictions: There are no direct contradictions; however, there is a disparity in the completeness of the reported information regarding sample geometry. One paper provides the context of repeated measurements for uncertainty, while the other explicitly states that sample geometry for specific values is not mentioned in the span.
cross_paper_synthesis.evidence_strength: Moderate. Both answers provide direct answers to procedural aspects (error definition, units) but lack full experimental details (e.g., exact sample dimensions in one case) to fully replicate the geometry.
cross_paper_synthesis.unresolved_gap: The specific sample geometry (dimensions, shape) used to calculate the reported mass gains (1.76, 4.45, and 9.08 mg/cm^2) is explicitly missing from the provided text for the second paper, preventing full geometric reproducibility.
cross_paper_synthesis.candidate_hypothesis: Mass gain normalization to surface area is standard practice for comparing oxidation rates across different durations and temperatures, but the lack of explicit geometric reporting in some studies limits the ability to correlate mass gain with volume loss or specific diffusion pathways.
cross_paper_synthesis.discriminating_experiment: A study should report mass gain alongside specific sample dimensions (length, width, thickness) and explicitly state whether the 'repeated measurements' for error bars involve distinct samples or the same sample measured multiple times over the duration.
